title: Splitting the Archive
setting: a records office split across buildings

post.author: u/glasshouse_nights_tabitha
post.title: I'm the night clerk in the newest of our county's record buildings. A birth registered on Monday was in none of them until Thursday, and I could see his box from my desk.

blocks.text: I file records at night for the Kelderby County Records Office. The archive outgrew one building long ago, so it's split by year: the Maltings holds 1850 to 1939, the Drill Hall 1940 to 1999, and the Glasshouse, mine, 2000 onward. Every record has a number, given in the order it was filed: 1,200,000 of them. A card at the front desk says which building holds which years. We call it the directory. Every lookup, every request for one record, goes through it in three steps. The desk looks the record's year up on the card. It asks the building the card names. That building checks its own shelves, and nowhere else.

Every new registration is dated this year, so every one comes to me. 1,200 arrive each night, and I can file 600. At dawn the other 600 wait by the door for the day shift. Across the lane the Maltings and the Drill Hall stand dark all night.

So on Monday 2 November the county opened a fourth building, the Ropewalk, and moved the boundary, the line between one building's years and the next. At noon Mr Lowther, the county archivist, changed the card: 2013 onward, the Ropewalk. The 120,000 records from 2013 on went across in vans, 30,000 a day, oldest boxes first, landing at 17:00, Monday to Thursday. From Monday night every new record went to the Ropewalk.

On Tuesday morning a mother came in for a copy of her son's birth certificate. He was registered on Monday at 09:12: No. 1,200,000, the last record filed in my building before noon. Below is the lookup log. Each line shows the day and time, then what was asked for or which van landed, then what the card or each building answered:

Tue 3 Nov 10:41  lookup No. 1,200,000   birth, registered Mon 2 Nov 09:12
                 directory              2013 onward: the Ropewalk
                 the Ropewalk           NOT FOUND
                 the Glasshouse         not our years
                 Maltings, Drill Hall   not our years
Wed 4 Nov 09:30  lookup No. 1,200,000   NOT FOUND in any building
Thu 5 Nov 17:00  van 4 of 4 shelved at the Ropewalk: 30,000 records
Thu 5 Nov 17:06  lookup No. 1,200,000   the Ropewalk: FOUND
Every building said it had never held him. On Tuesday night I could see his box on my shelf.

Nothing was lost. It just wasn't anywhere. The card had sent everyone to the Ropewalk before his box got there. Now the Ropewalk's night clerk leaves 600 at the door each dawn, and my nights are quiet. The county says it will need a fifth building within two years. Mr Lowther says the vans were too slow. What should he change before then?

blocks.label: directory_tuesday_1041.png

diagram.aria: Tabitha's drawing of Tuesday 3 November at 10:41. The front desk looks up record No. 1,200,000 and gets NOT FOUND. The directory, switched at noon on Monday, says 2013 onward: the Ropewalk. The Maltings holds 1850 to 1939 and the Drill Hall 1940 to 1999, both dark at night. The Ropewalk holds 2013 onward but has only 30,000 records so far, from van 1 of 4. The Glasshouse now holds 2000 to 2012 by the directory, but 90,000 records from 2013 on still sit on its shelves waiting for vans.

notes.text: Tuesday 10:41: 90,000 records from 2013 on sit in no building the directory names

blocks.caption: My drawing of Tuesday at 10:41. Since noon on Monday the directory has sent every record from 2013 on to the Ropewalk, but only Monday's van had landed: 30,000 records. The other 90,000 were still on the Glasshouse's shelves, and the Glasshouse turns away any year the directory doesn't give it. The Maltings and the Drill Hall hold their years and sit dark at night.

comments.author: u/grey_pager
comments.text: Your archive works like a database, the program that stores records, split over several machines. Each piece of a split like that is called a partition, or a shard. Three things to look at before anyone picks a fix. One: every split has a shard key, the one value that decides which building a record lives in. Yours is the year. Which year does every new record carry, so which building takes all of them, and what are the others doing at 03:00? Two: the directory. On Tuesday at 10:41, which building did it name for No. 1,200,000, and where was the box? Count how many records were in that state on Monday afternoon. Three: there will be a fifth building. For any rule you consider, ask how many of the 1,200,000 would ride in vans that week, how many would answer not found while they ride, and how many buildings someone asking for every record from 1931 would have to ask.

replies.author: u/glasshouse_nights_tabitha
replies.text: At noon on Monday, 120,000: everything from 2013 on. 90,000 on Tuesday morning. And something I forgot: in the spring the Ellingham family's solicitors bring in their deposit, 2,400 papers from 1931, all filed under one deposit number.

comments.author: u/shelfmark_hartwell
comments.text: Forty years in county archives. Giving each building a range of years is how archives have always worked, and for good reason: a researcher asks for 1931, and 1931 sits on one run of shelves in one building. Scatter a year across four buildings and every question becomes four errands. Your county's only mistake was moving 2013 to 2026 at all, with the card already pointing at the Ropewalk. Next time, move nothing. Open the new building empty on New Year's Day for the new year. Every year stays where it was filed, the directory only ever gains a line, and no box ever rides in a van.

comments.author: u/remainder_mirela
comments.text: Or drop the card. At my last job we had three databases, and each customer's rows, one line of data per record, lived on one of them. A hash is a fixed recipe that turns any value into a number, the same number every time, with similar values giving very different numbers. Mod means the remainder after dividing. So finding a row's home took three steps. Hash the customer id. Divide the number by 3 and keep the remainder. Go to the database with that number. We wrote it as hash(customer id) mod 3. Anyone can work it out on a scrap of paper, so there's no list to keep, and new rows spread evenly whatever year they carry.

comments.author: u/one_roof_fenella
comments.text: Honest answer from a parish office: we had the same mess across three halls, and in 2019 we moved everything into one old mill with room for twice what we had. One roof, one card, no boundaries between buildings, two clerks at night. It's still fine. It won't be fine forever, but it bought us years.

reply.prompt: Kelderby will need a fifth building within two years, and more after that. What should Mr Lowther change before then? Part 2 follows your advice.

options.text: Hash each record number into one of 120 fixed partitions; move whole ones to a new building, fixing the card as each lands.
options.part2: Mr Lowther rebuilt the archive over the winter as 120 fixed partitions. A record's partition is a hash of its number, each building holds 30, and the directory lists all 120. The switch itself was one big move: 900,000 of the 1,200,000 records changed building, because every record's place was decided again. He moved them a partition at a time, in three steps: copy the partition to its new building, then change that partition's line in the directory, then clear the old shelves. No lookup failed. Each partition keeps its own index by date, a sorted list that points straight to each year's records. Now each building files 300 a night and nobody waits at dawn. In March the Tannery opened: 24 whole partitions, 240,000 records, 8 vans, and nothing was unreachable for a minute. The price came in two places. A question for every record from 1931 now goes to all five buildings, every partition reading its by-date index, and the answer comes when the slowest building replies. And in April the Ellingham deposit arrived, 2,400 papers under one deposit number: one partition, so the Tannery got 2,640 records that night. Deposits are now keyed by deposit and item number, so each paper gets its own hash.
options.senior: Sharding splits both the storing and the writing, and the shard key decides everything after. Years keep a range of years in one place but send every new record to one building. A hash of the record number spreads the writes, at the price of asking every building whenever you want a range of years, so keep a by-date index in each partition. Many more fixed partitions than buildings make opening one a matter of moving whole partitions, a quarter of the records for a fourth building. And a directory switched one partition at a time keeps every record findable during the move. One hot key, a single value that gets far more records than the rest, still needs splitting.

options.text: Keep filing by year, but open each new building empty on New Year's Day for that year's records, so no box ever has to move again.
options.verdict: Moves nothing, still one hot building
options.part2: On 1 January the Tannery opened, empty, for 2027. Nothing moved, nothing went missing, and the directory gained one line. Then, on the first night of 2027, every new record went to the Tannery. Its night clerk files 600 of the 1,200, and 600 wait at dawn, while four buildings across the lane stand dark: busiest building 1,200 a night, average 240. In April the Ellingham deposit, 2,400 papers dated 1931, all went to the Maltings, which filed 600 and left 1,800 for the morning. The county is already asking what happens in 2028.
options.senior: Ranges by year keep each year in one place, and an empty building for a new year moves nothing. But dates only grow, so every new record still lands on one building. That overloaded piece is called a hot partition, and it just moves on 1 January. MongoDB, a popular database program, says it plainly in its guides: with a shard key that always increases, every new record goes to one chunk, its name for a piece, and the shard holding it becomes the bottleneck for writes, the one narrow point everything queues at. Ranges suit keys whose new values arrive spread out, not in order.

options.text: Send each record to building hash(record number) mod the number of buildings: an even spread, and no directory to keep updated.
options.part2: Over the winter every record went to building hash(record number) mod 4. That alone moved 900,000 of the 1,200,000 records, and with no directory to switch one piece at a time, each of them answered not found from the morning the rule changed until its van came. After that each building filed 300 a night, and nobody waited. In March the Tannery opened and the rule became mod 5: 960,000 records changed building, in 32 vans, and on the first morning all 960,000 were in no building anyone would look in. A question for 1931 goes to all five buildings.
options.senior: A hash spreads new records evenly, and mod N, the remainder after dividing by the number of buildings, needs no directory. But the number of buildings is inside the formula, so changing it reshuffles almost everything. Going from 3 to 4, a record stays only if its hash leaves the same remainder for both, one in four. The EVCache case in Season 2 met the same trap with cache keys, the names of saved copies kept for quick reading. Keep a fixed number of partitions, far more than buildings, and a directory of which building holds each, so a new building takes only whole partitions.

options.text: Move every record into one much bigger building with two night clerks: one place to look, and no boundary ever to move again.
options.verdict: Trade-off: works now, the ceiling returns
options.part2: In January the county leased the Wool Store, an old warehouse with shelves for 2,000,000 records, and hired a second night clerk. Forty vans moved all 1,200,000 records, and this time Mr Lowther switched the directory as each van landed, so nothing went missing. Two clerks file 1,200 a night and nobody waits. A question for 1931 goes to one building. It works. But at 1,200 a night the county files 438,000 records a year, so the last 800,000 shelves fill in under two years. And on the night of the Ellingham deposit in April, 3,600 records came in and 2,400 waited at dawn.
options.senior: One bigger machine, called scaling up, is the honest first answer: no shard key, no partitions, every question in one place, and nothing that crosses buildings. It buys time, not room. One building's shelves and one door are still the limits, and growth reaches them again. Copies wouldn't help either. Read replicas, from s2e12 and s3e05, are full copies of the database that answer reads. Each holds every record and takes every write, so they spread lookups, never writes or storage. Shard when growth will pass the biggest building you can get.

sim.title: Split the Kelderby archive
sim.lede: You're Mr Lowther at noon on Monday 2 November, with 1,200,000 records in three buildings, numbered in the order they were filed. Pick how records are split: by year, where a new building takes the newer half of the newest building's records (as now) or only the next year's; by a hash of the record number mod the number of buildings; by a hash of the record number into fixed partitions (12, 120 or 1,200), with the directory saying which building holds each partition; or into one bigger building with two night clerks. Open a building to add one: the sim works out which records must move, and vans carry 30,000 a day, landing at 17:00. Choose whether the directory switches at once (as now) or entry by entry as each piece lands. Each night 1,200 new records arrive, all dated this year, and a night clerk files 600; the vans carry only the records on the shelves at noon on Monday. Turn on the Ellingham deposit for 2,400 papers from 1931 under one deposit number, then key it by deposit and item number. Ask for every record from 1931, or look up No. 1,200,000. The sim's hash multiplies the record number by 7,919 and keeps the remainder after dividing by 1,200,000, which spreads consecutive numbers perfectly evenly; a real hash is only nearly even. Changing the split, the partitions or the directory replays from Monday noon. Click any box to see what it holds.
sim.tryThis: Try this: open a building and look up No. 1,200,000. It's in no building, and 120,000 records can't be found. Send vans until Thursday's lands, and look again. Switch the directory to entry by entry, which replays, and open again: nothing goes missing, but the Ropewalk still takes all 1,200 a night. Try hash mod buildings: 400 each, but opening a fourth moves 900,000 records. Then 120 fixed partitions: 300,000, a quarter. Ask for 1931 under each. Turn on the Ellingham deposit, then key it by item. Last, try 12 partitions and open a fifth building.

explain.oneLine: No record was lost. At noon on Monday the directory was switched for 120,000 records whose boxes were still on the Glasshouse's shelves, so each one sat in no building anyone would look in until its van landed. And splitting by year meant every new record still went to one building: now the Ropewalk.

steps.title: One building runs out of shelves and hands.
steps.text: A database, the program that stores records, has two limits on one machine that copies can't lift. One is how much it can store. The other is how many writes, new or changed records, it can take. Read replicas, from s2e12 and s3e05, are full copies that answer reads. They share the lookups, but each copy still holds every record and applies every write. Sharding, also called partitioning, splits the records instead. Each building, or machine, holds a part and takes the writes for that part. The shard key is the value that decides which part a record goes to. It decides everything after: where new records land, which questions one building can answer alone, and what moves when a building opens. Kelderby's shard key is the year.

steps.title: Ranges keep neighbours together, and dates run hot.
steps.text: Range partitioning gives each building a run of key values: 1850 to 1939, 1940 to 1999, 2000 onward. Records with nearby keys sit together. A range query asks for every record between two values, like every record from 1931. Here it takes three steps. Read the directory to find the one building whose run holds 1931. Go to the first 1931 record on its shelves. Read along until the year changes. That walk along the shelves is a range scan, and it happens in one building. But a key that only grows, like a date or a number given in order, sends every new record to the building with the newest range. That's a hot partition, one piece doing far more than its share. The Glasshouse got 1,200 a night while the average building got 400, and 600 waited at dawn. Opening the Ropewalk for 2013 onward didn't cure it. It moved it: 1,200 at the Ropewalk against an average of 300. MongoDB's guides, for a popular database program, say the same of a shard key that always increases: every new record goes to one chunk, its word for a piece, and the shard holding it becomes the bottleneck for writes.

steps.title: Hashes spread the writes, and range questions go everywhere.
steps.text: Hash partitioning puts a record where a hash of its key says. A hash is a fixed recipe that turns a value into a number, always the same number for the same value. Placing a record takes three steps. Work out the hash of its key. Turn that number into a partition, for example by keeping the remainder after dividing. Send the record there. Neighbouring record numbers land in different places, so new records spread evenly: 400 a building with three, 300 with four. The price is the range query. A record's number says nothing about its year, so every record from 1931 means asking every building. That's called scatter and gather, and it runs in steps. Send the same question to every building. Each searches its own shelves. Wait for every answer. Merge them into one list. The answer comes only when the slowest building replies, and if one building is down, the list is incomplete. An index is a sorted list that points to where each record sits. A by-date index inside each partition makes each building's share quick, but not the trips. And a hash can't spread one key that carries too much. The Ellingham deposit, 2,400 papers under one deposit number, lands on one partition: 2,700 tonight at the Ropewalk against an average of 900. Salting the key fixes that in steps. Add a second part to the key, here the item number, so deposit number plus item number. Each paper now hashes differently and the papers spread, 900 a building. To read the deposit back, ask every partition and gather the pieces, which costs a scatter and gather every time.

steps.title: Rebalancing: move whole partitions, and keep the directory honest.
steps.text: Rebalancing means moving records between machines so each holds a fair share. The simplest hash rule, building = hash mod the number of buildings, has the count inside the formula. Mod is the remainder after dividing. Change the count and almost everything moves, as the EVCache case warned for cache keys, the names of saved copies. From 3 to 4 buildings, a record stays only if its hash leaves the same remainder for both, one in four, so 900,000 of 1,200,000 records move. Instead, hash into a fixed number of partitions, many more than buildings, say 120. Keep a directory, also called a partition map, of which building holds each. A fourth building takes 30 whole partitions, a quarter of the records, 300,000, and no even split can move fewer. Route every lookup through the directory. Then move each partition in four steps. First, copy it to its new building; until the copy is done, lookups still go to the old one, which is fine. Next, catch up any records written to the old copy during the move; skip this and those records are left behind. Then switch the partition's entry in the directory; switch it before the copy lands and its records answer not found. Last, clear the old shelves; clear them while anything still sends records there and those records are lost. Kelderby switched the directory for 120,000 records at noon on Monday, while their boxes were still on the Glasshouse's shelves.

steps.title: Shard-aware IDs, and what sharding costs.
steps.text: An ID is the unique number a system gives each record. Instagram's 2012 IDs put the shard in the ID. Like the Snowflake-style numbers of s2e14, IDs built from the clock and a counter, they are 64-bit whole numbers. A bit is a single 0 or 1, so a 64-bit number is 64 of them in a row. Instagram builds each ID in three steps. First, 41 bits of time, counted in milliseconds, thousandths of a second. Next, 13 bits of logical shard ID, which piece the record lives in: up to 8,192 shards. Last, 10 bits of sequence, a counter for that shard that wraps round, so 1,024 IDs per shard per millisecond. Where Snowflake keeps a 10-bit machine number and a 12-bit count, Instagram keeps the shard. Its several thousand logical shards map to far fewer database servers, and moving a set of them to a new server changes no ID. Anything holding an ID knows its shard without asking. The cost of all sharding is work that crosses shards. A query without the shard key goes everywhere. A transaction, a group of changes the database makes all or nothing, as s3e02 covered, can't stay local once it changes records in two buildings. It needs a protocol, an agreed set of steps, such as two-phase commit. That runs in two rounds. First a coordinator asks every machine involved to get the change ready and say yes or no. Then, only if all said yes, it tells them all to make it count; otherwise it tells them all to cancel. If the coordinator fails between the rounds, the machines wait, holding their records. The other way out is a shard key chosen so records that change together live together.

diagram.aria: The fix, drawn for four buildings. The night intake, 1,200 new records a night, 300 to each building. The directory lists 120 fixed partitions and switches entry by entry as each partition lands. The Maltings, the Drill Hall, the Glasshouse and the Ropewalk each hold 30 partitions and take 300 new records a night. Opening a fifth building moves 24 whole partitions, 240,000 records, with none unreachable.

notes.text: Opening a fifth: 24 whole partitions, 240,000 records, none unreachable

explain.caption: The fix, drawn for four buildings. A record's partition is a hash of its number, and the directory says which building holds each of the 120 partitions: 30 each, so each building takes 300 of the night's 1,200. When a fifth building opens it takes 24 whole partitions, 240,000 records, and each partition's line in the directory changes only once its copy has landed.

fix.title: The fix: hash into 120 fixed partitions, move whole ones, switch the directory one entry at a time
fix.text: Make the shard key a hash of the record number, into 120 fixed partitions, and give each building 30. New records then spread evenly, 300 a building a night, and nobody waits at dawn. Keep an index by date inside each partition, so a question for a year is quick in each building, though it now goes to every building. Keep the directory as the one list of which building holds each partition, and send every lookup and every new record through it. When a building opens, move whole partitions to it, a quarter of the records for a fourth building and a fifth of them for a fifth, and for each partition copy first, switch its directory line once the copy has landed, and clear the old shelves last. Key anything that arrives in bulk under one number, like a family deposit, by its number and an item number, so it spreads too.

limits: Changing the shard key is itself one big move. Going from years to 120 hashed partitions decides every record's building again. With four buildings, 900,000 of the 1,200,000 records move once, the same three quarters a hash mod 4 would move. Plan it as a migration, a planned move of data, a partition at a time, not a weekend.

The number of partitions is a ceiling and a floor. 120 partitions can never spread over more than 120 buildings, and whole partitions divide unevenly when the count doesn't fit: 12 partitions over five buildings give 300 a night to two of them against an average of 240. Too many cost bookkeeping instead. PostgreSQL, a widely used database program, warns in its guide that too many partitions mean longer query planning, the time it spends working out how to answer a question, and more memory.

Hashing spreads keys, not one key. A deposit under one number, or one customer who writes far more than the rest, still lands on one partition. Salting it, adding a second part to the key, means every read of that key asks every piece. Questions that cross partitions get slower and harder. Every record from 1931 needs a scatter and gather. A change to two records in two buildings needs a cross-shard transaction, an all-or-nothing change spread over two machines.

explain.seniorTake: Shard when one machine can't hold the data or take the writes, and not before, because every split makes some questions harder. Then pick the shard key from how the data arrives and how it's asked for. Ranges keep neighbours together and answer a range in one place, but a key that only grows makes the newest range hot forever. A hash spreads the writes and sends every range question to every machine. Whatever you hash, hash into many more fixed partitions than machines, and keep a map of which machine holds each. Grow by moving whole partitions: copy first, catch up, and switch each map entry only once its copy has landed, so nothing is ever unreachable. Watch the busiest partition against the average, the mean, because one hot key beats any hash. And design so that records changed together share a shard.

realWorld.title: Instagram, 2012: thousands of logical shards, and the shard in the ID
realWorld.text: Instagram, the photo-sharing app, kept its data in PostgreSQL, a widely used database program. Its engineering blog described how it split that data into shards: "Our sharded system consists of several thousand ‘logical’ shards that are mapped in code to far fewer physical shards. Using this approach, we can start with just a few database servers, and eventually move to many more, simply by moving a set of logical shards from one database to another, without having to re-bucket any of our data." Each logical shard is a PostgreSQL schema, a named group of tables inside one database, and each split-up table exists inside each schema. Its IDs had to sort in time order, ideally fit in 64 bits, and add as few moving parts as possible. So it turned down a separate Snowflake service, a program that hands out IDs, and made IDs inside PostgreSQL. Each ID consists of "41 bits for time in milliseconds (gives us 41 years of IDs with a custom epoch)", "13 bits that represent the logical shard ID" and "10 bits that represent an auto-incrementing sequence, modulus 1024. This means we can generate 1024 IDs, per shard, per millisecond". Its worked example, where % means the remainder after dividing: "Let’s say we’re sharding by user ID, and there are 2000 logical shards; if our user ID is 31341, then the shard ID is 31341 % 2000 -> 1341." A primary key is the value that names each row uniquely. The post calls the result "Primary keys that are unique across our application (and as a bonus, contain the shard ID in them for easier mapping)." One number to check: 2^41 milliseconds is about 69.7 years, as s2e14 worked out, so the post's 41 years undersells its own layout.

realWorld.title: PostgreSQL: range, list and hash, inside one server
realWorld.text: PostgreSQL's documentation says "Partitioning refers to splitting what is logically one large table into smaller physical pieces." A table is a set of records laid out in rows. It offers three built-in forms. Range: "The table is partitioned into “ranges” defined by a key column or set of columns, with no overlap between the ranges of values assigned to different partitions. For example, one might partition by date ranges". List: "The table is partitioned by explicitly listing which key value(s) appear in each partition." Hash: "The table is partitioned by specifying a modulus and a remainder for each partition." On when it pays: "a rule of thumb is that the size of the table should exceed the physical memory of the database server." That means the table is bigger than the machine's fast working memory. On how many: "Too many partitions can mean longer query planning times and higher memory consumption", and if you choose one partition per customer while customers are few and large, "it may be better to choose to partition by HASH and choose a reasonable number of partitions". These partitions all live in one server. Sharding spreads the same idea over several.

realWorld.title: MongoDB: ranged sharding keeps neighbours together
realWorld.text: MongoDB's docs on ranged sharding: "Range-based sharding involves dividing data into contiguous ranges determined by the shard key values. In this model, documents with "close" shard key values are likely to be in the same chunk or shard. This allows for efficient queries where reads target documents within a contiguous range." MongoDB is a popular database program, and a chunk is its word for one piece of a split. The docs add that it works best with a shard key of large cardinality, many different values; low frequency, no value far more common than the rest; and values that don't change monotonically, meaning don't only grow.

realWorld.title: MongoDB: hashed sharding spreads them out
realWorld.text: MongoDB's docs on hashed sharding: "Hashed sharding provides a more even data distribution across the sharded cluster at the cost of reducing Targeted Operations vs. Broadcast Operations. Post-hash, documents with "close" shard key values are unlikely to be on the same chunk or shard - the mongos is more likely to perform Broadcast Operations to fulfill a given ranged query." The mongos is MongoDB's router, the part that passes each question to the right shards. A targeted operation goes to one shard; a broadcast goes to all of them. It adds that hashed keys "are ideal for shard keys with fields that change monotonically like ObjectId values or timestamps." An ObjectId is MongoDB's default record ID, and it starts with the time, so both only grow.

realWorld.title: MongoDB: keys that only grow, keys that repeat, and scatter-gather
realWorld.text: MongoDB's guide to choosing a shard key, where maxKey marks the top end of the last range: "If the shard key value is always increasing, all new inserts are routed to the chunk with maxKey as the upper bound." Then "The shard containing that chunk becomes the bottleneck for write operations." Its advice: "If your data model requires sharding on a key that changes monotonically, consider using Hashed Sharding." On repeated values: "If the majority of documents contain only a subset of the possible shard key values, then the chunks storing the documents with those values can become a bottleneck within the cluster." And on queries: "When the queries do not contain the shard key, the queries are broadcast to all shards for evaluation. These types of queries are called scatter-gather queries. Queries that involve multiple shards for each request are less efficient and do not scale linearly when more shards are added to the cluster."

realWorld.title: DynamoDB: each partition has a ceiling
realWorld.text: DynamoDB is AWS's database service, rented from Amazon's cloud. Its guide counts work in read and write units, and says "Every partition in a DynamoDB table is designed to deliver a maximum capacity of 3,000 read units per second and 1,000 write units per second." So the table's total throughput, the work it can do each second, only helps if the work spreads. The guide's first advice is: "You should design your application for uniform activity across all partition keys in the table and its secondary indexes."

realWorld.title: DynamoDB: dates make hot partitions
realWorld.text: The guide warns that "A partition key design that doesn't distribute I/O requests effectively can create "hot" partitions that result in throttling", and rates "Item creation date, rounded to the nearest time period (for example, day, hour, or minute)" as a Bad partition key. Throttling means the service turns requests away until the load drops, and the partition key is DynamoDB's name for the shard key. It also marks as Bad a device ID where one device "is by far more popular than all the others."

realWorld.title: DynamoDB: write sharding, and its cost
realWorld.text: The guide's fix is write sharding, adding a suffix, an ending, to a busy key so its writes spread: "for a partition key that represents today's date, you might choose a random number between 1 and 200 and concatenate it as a suffix to the date." The cost: "to read all the items for a given day, you would have to query the items for all the suffixes and then merge the results." A suffix calculated from the order ID instead lets you find one item directly, and either way "you avoid having a single "hot" partition key value taking all of the workload."

asked: How would you shard this table?
Range or hash partitioning: which would you use, and when?
How do you add a shard without downtime?
What's a hot partition, and how do you fix it?
interview.answer: First ask whether to shard at all. Replicas, full copies, spread reads. A bigger machine buys time. Sharding is for when one machine can't hold the data or take the writes. Then choose the shard key from the access patterns: how the data is written and asked for. It should spread writes, have many different values with none far more common than the rest, and put records that are read or changed together on the same shard. Range partitioning keeps neighbouring keys together, so range scans hit one shard. But a key that only grows, like a timestamp (the time a record was made) or an ID given in order, sends every new record to the newest shard. Hash partitioning spreads writes evenly, but range queries become scatter and gather across every shard, so keep a local index, such as by date, in each partition. Never use hash mod the number of servers: from 3 to 4 servers it moves about three quarters of the keys. Hash into a fixed number of partitions, far more than servers, and keep a partition map of which server holds each. Add a server by moving whole partitions in four steps: copy a partition, catch up the writes made meanwhile, switch its map entry, then delete the old copy. No key is ever unreachable and nothing needs downtime, a time when the service is switched off. Consistent hashing, the next case, is the other common answer. A hot partition is one shard taking far more traffic than the rest, from a growing key or from one hot key. Fix the first by hashing, and the second by salting the key with a suffix, or giving that key its own partition. Watch the busiest partition against the mean, the average. Mention shard-aware IDs, like Instagram's 13-bit logical shard ID, and the cost: cross-shard queries and transactions.

terms.def: A local government archive that keeps a county's registrations: births, marriages, deaths and deeds. Kelderby's is split across buildings.
Recording a birth, marriage, death or deed with the county. Each one becomes a record in the archive.
The number every Kelderby record gets, in the order it was filed, from 1 to 1,200,000. The Monday birth is No. 1,200,000.
The person who files the night's new records in one building. Each Kelderby night clerk files 600 a night.
The new records that reach Kelderby's buildings each night to be filed: 1,200, all dated this year.
The card at Kelderby's front desk that says which building holds which records. Every lookup goes through it. A partition map is the same idea.
Asking for one record by its number: the front desk reads the directory and asks the building it names.
How Kelderby moves records between buildings: 30,000 records a day, landing at 17:00.
A collection of papers handed to an archive in one go, often by a family or a firm, and filed under one deposit number.
2,400 papers from 1931 that the Ellingham family's solicitors bring in one night, all under one deposit number.
The value that decides which partition, and so which machine, a record lives in. Also called the partition key. Kelderby's is the year.
Giving each partition a run of key values, such as 1850 to 1939. Records with neighbouring keys sit together.
Putting each record where a hash of its key says. Neighbouring keys land in different partitions, so records spread evenly.
Hash the key, divide by N, the number of machines, and keep the remainder: that's the record's machine. No list needed, but when N changes, most records move.
A question for every record between two key values, such as every record from 1931.
Reading a run of neighbouring keys in order, from one place. Under range partitioning a range query is one range scan in one partition.
A key that only grows, such as a date, a timestamp or a number given in order. Under ranges every new record lands in the last partition.
MongoDB's phrase for a key whose values only go up, or only go down, like a date. It's the same as a sequential key.
Some key values carrying far more records or traffic than others, so their partition runs hot even when keys are hashed.
Adding a suffix, such as an item number, to a busy key so its records spread over several partitions. Reading them back means asking every piece.
A set number of partitions, many more than machines, chosen once. Machines hold whole partitions, and a new machine takes some of them whole.

A logical shard is one of many fixed pieces of the data. A physical shard is the server that holds several of them, like a building holding many boxes. Instagram puts thousands of logical shards on far fewer servers.
Instagram's word for deciding again which shard every record belongs to, as changing hash mod N does. Moving whole logical shards avoids it.
A table of which machine holds each partition, read to route every request. Kelderby's directory is one.
Sending each request to the machine that holds its record, by a rule such as hash mod N or by reading a partition map.
Moving partitions or records between machines so each holds a fair share, as when a machine is added or removed.
The order for moving a partition with nothing unreachable: copy it to its new home, switch its map entry, then clear the old copy.
A record the directory sends to a building that doesn't have it yet. The sim counts these as records nobody can find right now.
The sim's hash: 7,919 times the record number, keeping the remainder after dividing by 1,200,000. It spreads consecutive numbers perfectly evenly; a real hash is only nearly even.
The sim's measure of a hot partition: the most new records any building gets tonight against the mean. An even spread makes them equal.
Asking every partition the same question, waiting for all the answers, then merging them into one. It's as slow as the slowest partition. MongoDB calls these scatter-gather queries.
MongoDB's names for queries sent to every shard and queries sent only to the shard that holds the key.
A sorted list of dates inside each partition, pointing to where each record sits, so it can find one year's records without reading them all. Like a book's index.
A query that needs records from more than one shard, so it must ask several and merge the answers.
An all-or-nothing group of changes that touches records on more than one shard. One machine can't make it happen alone, so it needs agreed steps between machines, such as two-phase commit.

Two rounds of steps. First a coordinator asks every machine to get a change ready. Then, only if all said yes, it tells them all to make it count. Slower, and stuck if the coordinator fails between rounds.
An ID that carries its shard's number, so anything holding it can tell where the record lives. Instagram's IDs hold 13 bits of logical shard ID.
The last 10 bits of an Instagram ID: a counter that goes up by one each time and wraps back round to the start, so one shard can make 1,024 IDs a millisecond.
A photo-sharing app. Its engineers described sharding PostgreSQL and making shard-aware IDs in 2012.
A named group of tables inside one PostgreSQL database, like a labelled drawer in a cabinet. Each Instagram logical shard is one, so one server can hold many.
Splitting one table into partitions inside one PostgreSQL server, by range, list or hash. It doesn't spread the table across servers.
A popular database program that stores records as documents. It can spread them over many shards, by ranges or by hashes of a shard key.
MongoDB's word for one piece of a split: a range of shard key values and the records in it, like one shelf run. MongoDB moves chunks between shards to even them out.
MongoDB's marker for a value above every other shard key value. The last piece's range runs up to it, so a key that only grows keeps landing there.
Cardinality is how many different values a shard key has; frequency is how often each one turns up. Few values, or a few very common ones, make pieces that can't spread.
MongoDB's router, like a front desk. A question that names the shard key goes to the one shard holding it; a question without the key goes to every shard.
MongoDB's default record ID, 12 bytes long. It starts with the time it was made, so new ones only grow.
An extra sorted list on a DynamoDB table, so items can be found by some other detail, not just the table's own key. Like a second card index sorted by a different field.
Short for input and output: the reading and writing a database does to its storage, the disks that keep data with the power off.
One app serving many customers, called tenants, from shared machines and databases, like flats in one block.
Software as a service: an app a company rents to its customers over the web instead of selling them a copy.
A rule in ISO/IEC 27001:2022, a security standard companies are checked against. It expects you to watch how much of your machines you use and plan ahead, so you never run out of room.

atWork: Picture a multi-tenant SaaS product: software rented over the web, serving many customer companies from shared machines. It put each customer's rows on one of eight PostgreSQL databases by a hash of the customer id. It ran evenly for two years. Then its biggest customer ran a year-end import, loading a whole year of data at once. One database sat at 95% CPU, its processor nearly flat out, while seven idled, and every smaller customer sharing that database waited. The fix the team wanted, a ninth database by hash mod 9, would have moved almost every row. Look for both in your own systems. For each sharded or partitioned store, from PostgreSQL partitions to DynamoDB tables to a MongoDB cluster, a group of machines working as one, write down the shard key. Then measure the busiest partition against the average, not just the total. DynamoDB's CloudWatch Contributor Insights, from s2e11, a monitoring view, shows the most-used partition keys. In PostgreSQL, a count of rows per partition shows the skew, how uneven they are. Ask whether the key only grows, as dates and order numbers do, and whether one tenant can outgrow a partition. Then read how a shard is added: is it hash mod N, or whole partitions moved under a map, and does the map switch before or after the data lands? If you are heading for Build Night L4, the Loadout data tier, rehearse this before you build. Make one key uneven on purpose: give it forty times the writes of the rest, and watch its partition run hot. Then salt it, adding a suffix, and watch the busiest partition fall back towards the average. If your company is pursuing ISO/IEC 27001:2022, a security standard, control A.8.6 (capacity management) expects the use of resources to be monitored and future capacity needs projected. Load per partition against the average, and a written plan for adding a shard before the busiest one fills, are the kind of evidence an auditor asks for. Build them in now rather than at audit time.

recall.prompt: An app that serves many customer companies keeps its orders in four PostgreSQL databases. It picks each order's database by hash(customer id) mod 4: hash the customer id, divide by 4, keep the remainder. A retailer runs a flash sale, a few hours of cut prices, and its database sits at 95% CPU, its processor nearly flat out, while the other three idle. Next month the team wants a fifth database. What's going on, and what would you change?

keyIdeas.idea: One customer's key carries most of the writes: a hot partition from key skew, and no hash can spread a single key
Split or salt that customer's key across several partitions, or give it a partition of its own
Going from mod 4 to mod 5 moves about four fifths of the rows; hash into many fixed partitions with a map instead, and move whole partitions

recall.model: The retailer is a hot key, one value carrying far more work than the rest. Every one of its orders has the same customer id, so the same hash and the same database. That's a hot partition from key skew, and no hash can spread a single key. Split that customer's key, for example customer id plus a suffix from 1 to 8 taken from the order number. Its orders then spread over several partitions, at the cost of asking all of them to list its orders. Or give a customer that big its own shard. And don't go to mod 5: changing the count moves about four fifths of the rows, and each is unreachable until it lands. Hash into a fixed number of partitions, far more than databases, and keep a partition map of which database holds each. Then move whole partitions to the fifth database, one at a time: copy it first, then switch its map entry once the copy has landed, then clear the old copy.

recall.prompt: Records go to building hash(record number) mod the number of buildings, and the hash spreads them evenly. A fourth building joins three. Roughly what share of the records changes building?
options: None: only new records go to the new building
recall.why: A record stays only if its hash leaves the same remainder divided by 3 and by 4, which happens for 3 of every 12 values: a quarter stay and three quarters move. In the sim, 900,000 of 1,200,000. A quarter is what moving whole fixed partitions costs, and it's the least any even split can move.

recall.prompt: Instagram's 2012 post describes 64-bit IDs made inside PostgreSQL. How are the bits split?
options: 41 bits of time, 10 bits of machine number, 12 bits of count
41 bits of time, 13 bits of logical shard ID, 10 bits of sequence
48 bits of time, then the rest random
32 bits of shard ID, then 32 bits of auto-increment
recall.why: The post lists 41 bits for time in milliseconds, 13 bits that represent the logical shard ID, and 10 bits of an auto-incrementing sequence, modulus 1024: 1,024 IDs per shard per millisecond. The first choice is the Snowflake-style layout of s2e14. Instagram put the shard where the machine number was, so any ID says which logical shard holds its row.

recall.prompt: A table of sensor readings is split across 6 shards by ranges of timestamp, the time each reading was taken. What happens to new writes, and to a query for one hour of readings?
options: Writes spread evenly, and the hour's query asks all 6 shards
Writes spread evenly, and the hour's readings sit on one shard
Every new reading lands on the newest shard, and the hour's readings sit on one shard
Every new reading lands on a random shard, and the hour's query asks all 6 shards
recall.why: Timestamps only grow, so with ranges every insert goes to the shard holding the newest range, a hot partition, as at the Glasshouse. In exchange, an hour of readings is one range scan on one shard. Hashing the timestamp would spread the writes and turn the hour's query into scatter and gather.

recall.prompt: You're moving one partition to a new server while the app keeps running. In which order should the steps go?
options: Switch its map entry, copy the partition, then clear the old copy
Switch the whole map at once, then copy the partitions over a few days
Copy the partition, switch its map entry, then clear the old copy
Clear the old copy, then copy the partition and switch its map entry
recall.why: Copy first, so the new home holds everything before anyone is sent there; switch the entry, so lookups go to the copy; clear the old copy last. Switching first, for one partition or all of them, leaves those records unreachable until they land, as Kelderby's directory did for 120,000 records. Real systems also catch up the writes made during the copy just before the switch.

coldCase.update: UPDATE, 8 months later. Kelderby runs on 120 fixed partitions now, and in June the Coach House opened as the sixth building. Mr Lowther moved its 20 partitions one at a time: copy, change the partition's line in the directory, clear the old shelves. Lookups never failed. But the night intake desk sorts each night's sacks by its own printed copy of the directory, which it prints on Mondays. On Wednesday night it filed 312 new records at the buildings its printout named, for partitions that had moved to the Coach House on Tuesday. On Thursday the day staff cleared those partitions' old shelves into the basement store, as the plan said, and the 312 went with them. On Friday a man came in for his marriage certificate, registered on Wednesday. No building has it.
coldCase.prompt: Reply to OP. What happened, and what should Mr Lowther change?

keyIdeas.idea: The intake desk routed by an out-of-date copy of the directory, so new records went to a partition's old home after its entry had switched
One directory as the source of truth, read for every new record; a building refuses or forwards records for partitions it no longer holds
Recover the records from the cleared shelves and file them in their partitions; clear an old home only after its last writes are caught up and nothing can be sent there

coldCase.model: The intake desk filed Wednesday's records by its Monday printout, a stale, out-of-date copy of the directory. So 312 records went to the old homes of partitions that had already moved and whose entries had already switched. Every lookup then went to the Coach House, which never got them, and the old shelves were cleared with those records on them. Make one directory the source of truth: the intake desk reads it for every sack, never a weekly copy, and a building refuses, or forwards, any record for a partition it no longer holds, so a stale copy fails loudly instead of quietly. Clear an old home only after its last write has been caught up and nothing can still be sent there. Then go through the cleared boxes, recover the 312 records and file them in their partitions.

next: Next, The Ring: a carousel that never stops, and placing keys on machines with consistent hashing and virtual nodes.

sources.title: Instagram Engineering, Sharding & IDs at Instagram (2012; dated 30 December 2012 on its Medium blog), read in the Internet Archive's copy of 12 January 2021, because the live address could not be reached when this case was written (several thousand logical shards mapped in code to far fewer physical shards; moving a set of logical shards without re-bucketing; each logical shard a Postgres schema; 41 bits for time in milliseconds, 13 bits of logical shard ID, 10 bits of auto-incrementing sequence modulus 1024; the 2000 logical shards and user 31341 example)

PostgreSQL 18 documentation, 5.12 Table Partitioning (splitting one large table into smaller physical pieces; range, list and hash partitioning; the rule of thumb that the table should exceed the server's physical memory; too many partitions mean longer query planning and more memory; one partition per customer against HASH with a reasonable number of partitions)
MongoDB Database Manual, Ranged Sharding (contiguous ranges of shard key values; close values likely in the same chunk or shard; efficient queries over a contiguous range)

MongoDB Database Manual, Hashed Sharding (a more even data distribution at the cost of targeted operations; close values unlikely on the same shard; broadcast operations for ranged queries; ideal for keys that change monotonically like ObjectId values or timestamps)

MongoDB Database Manual, Choose a Shard Key (cardinality, frequency, monotonically changing keys; always-increasing keys route all inserts to the maxKey chunk, whose shard becomes the write bottleneck; scatter-gather queries are broadcast to all shards)

Amazon DynamoDB Developer Guide, Designing partition keys to distribute your workload in DynamoDB (hot partitions result in throttling; item creation date rounded to a time period, and one far more popular device, rated Bad)

Amazon DynamoDB Developer Guide, Using write sharding to distribute workloads evenly in your DynamoDB table (a random suffix from 1 to 200 on the date; querying every suffix and merging the results; calculated suffixes from the order ID; avoiding a single hot partition key value)

Amazon DynamoDB Developer Guide, Best practices for designing and using partition keys effectively in DynamoDB (each partition designed to deliver a maximum of 3,000 read units and 1,000 write units per second; design for uniform activity across partition keys)

UpGuard: ISO 27001 Control 8.6, Capacity Management (a summary of the control, not the standard's own text: monitor the utilization of system resources and project future capacity requirements so adequate resources stay available)
